summary: Two days before Passover, Jesus foretells His betrayal; the chief priests plot to seize Him quietly, and Judas Iscariot agrees to hand Him over for money.
key_insight: The council said, “Not during the feast.” Jesus had just said that after two days, at the Passover, the Son of Man would be delivered up to be crucified. Judas’s offer changed the leaders’ plans, but the timetable kept was Jesus’, not theirs.
story: When Jesus had finished all these sayings, He told His disciples, “You know that after two days is the Passover, and the Son of Man will be delivered up to be crucified.” {Mt}

The Feast of Unleavened Bread, called Passover, was drawing near. {Lk} The chief priests, the scribes and the elders of the people gathered at the palace of the high priest, Caiaphas, {Mt} and looked for a way to take Jesus by trickery and kill Him. They feared the people, {Lk} so they said, “Not during the feast, lest there be an uproar among the people.” {Mt}

Then Satan entered Judas, surnamed Iscariot, who was numbered among the twelve. {Lk} He went to the chief priests and the captains of the temple guard {Lk} and asked, “What are you willing to give me if I deliver Him to you?” {Mt} They were glad, and agreed to give him money. {Lk} They counted out to him thirty pieces of silver. {Mt}
From that time Judas looked for an opportunity to betray Jesus {Mt} when the crowds were not around. {Lk}
differences: Only Matthew records Jesus’ words, “after two days is the Passover,” and names Caiaphas’s palace as the meeting place.
Only Luke says that Satan entered Judas and that Judas also conferred with the temple “captains.”
Matthew alone records Judas’s question and the price, “thirty pieces of silver”; Mark and Luke say only that the leaders promised him money.

Matthew and Mark tell of the anointing at Bethany between the plot and Judas’s visit (Matthew 26:6–13; Mark 14:3–9), though John sets that supper just after Jesus arrived six days before the Passover; Luke has no anointing here.

scene.label: Thirty pieces of silver
scene.text: The Law set thirty shekels of silver as the payment for a slave gored by an ox (Exodus 21:32). In Zechariah 11:12–13, the shepherd rejected by the people is paid “thirty pieces of silver,” which Zechariah calls with bitter irony “that princely price.” Matthew later ties Judas’s money to that prophecy (Matthew 27:9–10).

scene.label: The captains
scene.text: The temple had its own guard, commanded by officers Luke calls “captains” (compare Acts 4:1). These were men who could make an arrest, and some of them came with Judas to Gethsemane (Luke 22:52).

scene.label: Passover crowds
scene.text: Jerusalem swelled with pilgrims at Passover, and Josephus tells of Roman soldiers posted on the temple porticoes during the feasts to stop riots. Many pilgrims were Galileans who had welcomed Jesus days before. The leaders had good reason to fear an uproar.

scene.label: The two days
scene.text: The Jewish day began at sunset. If Jesus spoke on Tuesday evening, as many think, it was already Wednesday by Jewish reckoning, and the two days ran to the Passover meal on Thursday evening. The Gospels do not say exactly when Judas went to the priests.

witnesses.matthew: Opens with Jesus Himself announcing the day and the manner of His death before His enemies even meet. Only Matthew gives the exact price, thirty pieces of silver, which he will trace back to the prophets when Judas throws it down (27:3–10). In Matthew, the King is never taken by surprise.
witnesses.mark: Is brief and stark: the leaders seek a way, Judas goes to them, and “they were glad.” Their problem, how to seize Jesus without a riot, had been solved by one of His own, and Mark twice names Judas “one of the twelve” (14:10, 43).
witnesses.luke: Alone names the power behind the betrayal: “Satan entered Judas.” After the temptation, the devil had left Jesus “until an opportune time” (4:13); now that time has come. Luke also notes the temple captains and Judas’s plan to act “in the absence of the multitude.”

seeing.reveals: Jesus is not caught in a plot; He names the day before His enemies set it. Men bargain over His life with stealth and silver, but the Son of Man goes to the cross at the Passover, as He said and as God had planned.
seeing.living: Judas had walked with Jesus through His whole ministry and still sold Him for money. Being near Jesus is not the same as loving Him. Be honest with Him about any love, for money or anything else, that competes for your heart, and take courage that no back-room plan can move His appointed hour.
seeing.ponder: Is there anything you would quietly accept in exchange for your loyalty to Jesus?

preaching.big_idea: Men plotted and bargained, but Jesus went to the cross on God’s timetable, not theirs.
outline: The Lord who names His hour (1–2)
A disciple who sets a price (14–16)
preaching.watch_for: Matthew 26:2 is the fourth time in Matthew that Jesus foretells His death (16:21; 17:22–23; 20:18–19), and the first time He names the day. The leaders then say, “Not during the feast” (26:5). The reader knows whose word will stand.

title: The Plot and Judas’s Bargain
